video_title: Can South Korea Rescue America's Nuclear Renaissance? w/ Dr. Eunjung Lim
gist: Korea scholar Eunjung Lim explains how state-led industrial policy and never-stopped construction (including KEDO and Barakah) gave Korea its nuclear cost and delivery edge, and why Korea now sees the US as its key market after the Westinghouse-KEPCO settlement reportedly ceded Europe. The proposed ~$120B Korea-US framework (six AP1000s, possibly two APR1400s) hinges on Korean construction and heavy-forging capacity that the US lacks, but faces US political uncertainty and Korean demographic labor constraints.

insights.claim: A Korea-US nuclear framework reportedly envisions roughly $120 billion of Korean investment into the US to build six Westinghouse AP1000s and possibly two Korean APR1400 reactors.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Signals a potential large Korean-funded US new-build pipeline spanning both Westinghouse and KEPCO designs.
insights.quote: a possible 120 billion uh USD investment uh in some way, shape, or form from Korea into into the US to build uh six AP1000s, possibly two APR1400 uh reactors

insights.claim: Allowing APR1400s in the US would be a notable reversal, because the Westinghouse-KEPCO global settlement had reportedly barred South Korea from the American and European markets.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Any US APR1400 approval would effectively reopen the market division agreed in the IP settlement.

insights.claim: Lim is cautious on whether the US deal materializes, citing an 'absent-minded' America distracted by Middle East conflicts and Republican weakness ahead of midterms two weeks away.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: US political risk (midterms) could delay or dilute the Korea-US nuclear deal; details remain unresolved.
insights.quote: America is now very absent-minded, I think, with many things

insights.claim: If the global settlement really ceded Europe to Westinghouse, Korean nuclear industry and finance people broadly view the US as the market Korea must pursue, since other export options are narrow.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean suppliers have strong incentive to accept terms to win US work, shaping negotiating dynamics.
insights.quote: If American market is really the market we should we should really pursue, right?

insights.claim: US nuclear construction capability is the key bottleneck: Westinghouse has strong technology and Bechtel is strong, but construction execution is lacking in the US.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean EPC/construction capability is the scarce input in the US nuclear revival.
insights.quote: But, still construction is a really bottleneck here in this country.

insights.claim: Large heavy forgings such as reactor pressure vessels are effectively not producible in the US today, and restoring that capability would take time, forcing the US into partnerships.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Heavy-forging suppliers (e.g., Doosan) hold pricing power and strategic leverage in US new build.
insights.quote: it's not not just difficult, it's not even possible these days, I mean in in this country

insights.claim: Doosan Enerbility (formerly Doosan Heavy Industries, originally a public enterprise) produces gas turbines, wind turbines and reactor components at a single site with its own shipping yard, a one-stop facility Lim calls a Korean competitive advantage.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Doosan is positioned as a key beneficiary of US nuclear and gas-turbine demand.
insights.quote: So, it's a one-stop facility, really.

insights.claim: Lim judges Korea's negotiating position with the US has improved versus the time of the global settlement, with both sides sharing a loose consensus not to fight over every project.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Reduced Westinghouse-KEPCO litigation risk supports joint bids and Korean participation in US projects.
insights.quote: both sides have a loose consensus on that again that they should not fight over and over and over for every project

insights.claim: The Westinghouse-Korea relationship is described as fundamentally complementary, with Rosatom and Chinese state enterprises framed as the stronger competitors that make infighting counterproductive.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Western-allied consolidation against Russia/China is the strategic logic behind Westinghouse-KEPCO cooperation.

insights.claim: There is an active debate over whether Korea should receive a 5%, 10% or 25% stake in Westinghouse in connection with its confidential IPO.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: A Korean equity stake in Westinghouse is a live variable in the IPO and alliance structure.
insights.quote: And there's debate about should they get 5% 10% 25%?

insights.claim: Western nuclear finance contacts view a Korea-Westinghouse pairing as a 'dream team' in which Korea delivers construction and heavy components for US technology, as it did at Barakah.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Investor optimism on US nuclear rests heavily on Korean execution being imported.
insights.quote: This is a dream team.

insights.claim: Westinghouse's ownership is Canadian in origin, which Lim notes makes Canada a party in the Korea-US nuclear game as well.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Canadian owners of Westinghouse are stakeholders in any Korean partnership or stake deal.

themes.theme: Westinghouse-KEPCO IP dispute and market division

insights.claim: Korea's reactor lineage (KSNP, later OPR1000, then APR1400) traces back to Combustion Engineering technology, which later merged into Westinghouse, and this is the origin of the IP dispute.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Westinghouse's IP claim over Korean designs is structural, giving it ongoing leverage over Korean exports.
insights.quote: you're going to meet the Combustion Engineering, which was why we which was merged uh later into the Westinghouse. So, that's the origin of all this disputes

insights.claim: The most controversial reported term of the Westinghouse-KEPCO global settlement in Korea is a market division in which Westinghouse takes the European market, attacked by the opposition in National Assembly hearings.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean exporters may be locked out of Europe, the richest new-build market, creating domestic political pressure.
insights.quote: And the most controversial part was the market division right in South Korea.

insights.claim: Per the host's understanding, the settlement gave South Korea Africa, Latin America, some Asian countries and a carve-out for the Czech Republic, while Westinghouse got the countries that can actually pay for reactors.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: KEPCO's addressable export market is skewed toward less creditworthy buyers.
insights.quote: Westinghouse gets the gold in terms of countries that actually have the money to pay for the reactors

insights.claim: Korean industry people are very cautious about discussing the Westinghouse deal and do not want to ruin the relationship, so much of what is known comes from Korean press leaks and National Assembly hearings.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Deal terms remain opaque; information edge comes from Korean domestic political disclosures.

insights.claim: At Barakah, Westinghouse was disqualified but earned risk-free revenue via scope, royalties and reportedly future fuel contracts; at Dukovany it competed, was again disqualified early, and this triggered the IP conflict.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Westinghouse litigates when it is a direct competitor rather than a subcontractor, explaining the shift from cooperation to conflict.

insights.claim: Some have likened the Westinghouse-KEPCO global settlement agreement to a 'Monroe Doctrine' for resolving the IP dispute.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Framing of the deal as a spheres-of-influence arrangement.

themes.theme: Why Korea controls nuclear costs: continuous build

insights.claim: Korea's nuclear cost control stems from an ecosystem built over time that survived because Korea never stopped new nuclear construction, domestically or abroad.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Continuous build programs, not design alone, preserve the supply chain and keep costs down — a lesson for the US.
insights.quote: we actually never stopped the construction, right? So that's that's a really big thing.

insights.claim: Even under President Moon Jae-in's phase-out push, generation did not fall much and construction of Shin Kori 5 and 6 resumed after a public deliberative process.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean anti-nuclear policy shifts have had limited real impact on build continuity.
insights.quote: He was trying to again the stop the construction of Shin Kori 5 and 6, but at after all this public discussion and deliberative process again the construction were resumed ultimately.

insights.claim: Continuous construction let small and medium-sized Korean component manufacturers and chaebol subcontractors survive, which Lim calls the key difference between Korea and Japan.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Japan's post-Fukushima freeze destroyed supply chain continuity that Korea retained.

insights.claim: Lovering, Yip and Nordhaus's analysis of nuclear cost escalation is cited as showing Korea, unlike basically every other country with a fleet, kept nuclear costs down.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Korea is the empirical counterexample to nuclear cost escalation.

insights.claim: Lim worries Korea's nuclear ecosystem faces a looming skilled-labor shortage because the super-aged society cannot replace retiring skilled blue-collar workers, prompting talk of bringing retirees back.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean delivery capacity for US projects may be constrained by demographics.
insights.quote: Why don't we just bring back all this not all but retired again the people

insights.claim: Moon Jae-in's anti-nuclear slogan caused popularity of nuclear engineering at distinguished Korean universities to decline severely, a mistake Lim says must not be repeated.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Policy signals have lagged effects on the nuclear talent pipeline.

insights.claim: Keefer argues nuclear energy is vulnerable because it depends on highly skilled human resources while key builders (Korea, Japan, China, Russia) all face demographic decline, and Japan's nuclear industry has been frozen for 15 years post-Fukushima.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Workforce scarcity is a systemic constraint on global nuclear scale-up.
insights.quote: it strikes me that nuclear energy is in trouble if it's so dependent on highly skilled human resources

insights.claim: Lim's answer to the workforce problem is localization in export partnerships—transferring operating know-how and building local skilled labor in host countries—while noting AI and humanoid robots can substitute for some but not all work.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Workforce development in host countries (including the US) will be part of Korean deal structures.

themes.theme: Barakah and KEDO: Korea's export track record

insights.claim: KEDO, established after the Geneva Agreed Framework, had KEPCO as project manager building Korean standard reactors in North Korea; about 35% of construction was completed before termination in 2002-2003.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korea's first overseas build experience came from an aborted multilateral nonproliferation project.
insights.quote: Almost the 35% of the KEPCO construction was completed

insights.claim: KEDO taught Korean industry multilateral project management, producing thousands of official documents in English and working to international IAEA licensing guidelines, which became a precursor to Barakah.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Tacit export know-how compounds across projects, even failed ones.

insights.claim: Lim argues countries desperate for nuclear power when gas, solar or hydro are available should prompt suspicion of weapons intent, a lesson from North Korea that still applies today.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Nonproliferation screening heuristic for new-entrant nuclear programs.

insights.claim: Pyun Joon-young, who lived in North Korea managing KEDO and later led Barakah, was the key figure in Korea's export history and reported directly by phone to the president during Barakah.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean nuclear exports have been run with top-down presidential involvement.

insights.claim: The UAE disqualified Westinghouse's AP1000 early in the Barakah bid, prioritizing demonstrated construction track record, technological maturity and cost control over cutting-edge passive safety.
insights.speaker: Chris Keefer
insights.so_what: Buyers reward execution track record over design novelty, favoring KEPCO.

insights.claim: The Barakah win under President Lee Myung-bak, a former Hyundai Construction CEO, reflected a developmental-state approach and Gulf states' confidence from decades of Korean construction projects in the Middle East, which earned Korea foreign currency.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korea's EPC reputation in the Gulf underpins its nuclear export competitiveness.
insights.quote: This is another like a very I think a developmental state style approach.

insights.claim: Barakah's workforce spanned 34 nationalities without a common language, and veterans said it was more complicated than KEDO in North Korea.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean managers have demonstrated execution of highly complex multinational megaprojects.

insights.claim: Korea-UAE ties broadened beyond nuclear into defense, including exports of Cheongung air defense systems that Lim says worked during recent Iranian attacks.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Nuclear exports are bundled with comprehensive defense partnerships; France offers similar packages.
insights.quote: So actually Cheongung did work actually during the attack I mean the by Iran these days

insights.claim: Korea's nuclear program was born from energy scarcity: the peninsula's division left the South a de facto island cut off from northern hydro and coal, with all energy imported by sea.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Energy security, not just climate, anchors durable Korean support for nuclear.

insights.claim: Park Chung-hee's development strategy is described as a 'comparative advantage defying' model, assigning chaebol to sectors (Hyundai to autos, POSCO to steel, Samsung to electronics) and treating nuclear as a strategic asset.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: State-directed industrial policy is the template behind Korea's nuclear capability.
insights.quote: comparative advantage defying model

insights.claim: Lim attributes Korea's state-led success, unlike the Soviet Union, to an existential external threat that created survivalism and to a Confucian legacy of familiarity with strong bureaucrats.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Western attempts at copying Asian industrial policy may lack the cultural/strategic preconditions.

insights.claim: Despite nuclear's association with the controversial developmental state, Korean public polling today is quite positive on nuclear because energy-intensive industries like semiconductors depend on electricity.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Durable domestic political support for nuclear in Korea, driven by semiconductor power demand.
insights.quote: without semiconductor, again, our whole economy will be crumbling down

insights.claim: Korea's 'MASGA' (Make American Shipbuilding Great Again) and 'MANGA' (nuclear) collaborations enjoy general consensus in Korea, whereas investment in Alaska LNG is the more controversial part of the US deal.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean commitment to Alaska LNG is politically shakier than to nuclear or shipbuilding.
insights.quote: the news actually that became more controversial in Korea was actually Alaska LNG rather than nuclear

insights.claim: Skepticism about Alaska LNG in Korea rests on doubts that Korean gas demand can be sustained given slowing growth and a shrinking population, though another camp argues AI data centers will need gas; Lim personally favors engaging.
insights.speaker: Eunjung Lim
insights.so_what: Korean LNG demand outlook is contested, a risk for Alaska LNG offtake.
insights.quote: I personally do think um we should engage in that project
